funFact.value: Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan launched both Sputnik 1 in 1957 and Yuri Gagarin, the first human in space, in 1961.
funFact.note: 118 characters. Wikipedia confirms both launches from Baikonur; the site is leased to Russia.

driveSide.note: Listed as RHT; matches seed leftHand=false.

flag.text: Adopted in 1992 after independence from the Soviet Union, designed by Shaken Niyazbekov. Officially the light blue means a clear sky, peace and prosperity. The gold sun means wealth and life, and its rays are shaped like grains, a sign of plenty. The soaring steppe eagle, an old Kazakh symbol, means the power and independence of the state. The gold pattern on the left edge is a traditional ram's horn design honoring Kazakh art and culture.

reasons.feature: Adoption in 1992 and designer Shaken Niyazbekov
reasons.why: The presidential site (akorda.kz) confirms the flag was officially adopted in 1992 and designed by Shaken Niyazbekov; Wikipedia gives the date as 4 June 1992, chosen in a government contest.

The presidential site says the blue means pure sky, peace and prosperity, and also honesty, fidelity and integrity. Wikipedia adds that blue is traditionally significant to Turkic peoples and recalls the sky and water.

Official page (checked): the sun symbolizes wealth and abundance, life and energy; that is why the rays have the form of grain, a symbol of wealth and welfare. The official page gives no ray count; the 32 rays and their popular link to Turkic ethnic groups come from Wikipedia only.

Official page (checked): the eagle represents the power of the state, its sovereignty and independence, aspiration to high goals and a sustainable future. Wikipedia: eagles appeared on the flags of Kazakh tribes for centuries and stand for freedom.

reasons.feature: Gold ornament strip on the left edge
reasons.why: Official page (checked): the vertical band of national ornamental patterns represents the art and cultural traditions of the people of Kazakhstan. The name koshkar-muiz (ram's horns) and the change from red to gold in July 1992 come from Wikipedia, not the official page.

entries.remainingDoubts: Population is the WPP 2024 mid-2024 value as reproduced by Worldometers; the UN data portal itself could not be opened (HTTP 401). Charyn Canyon was not verified against a source. The exact adoption date 4 June 1992, the 32-ray count and the ram's horn name rest on Wikipedia; the official akorda.kz page confirms designer, year and meanings but not those details. Wikipedia's area list carries a footnote on Kazakhstan whose text was not retrieved; the figure used is the list's total including inland water.

funFact.value: Lake Issyk-Kul sits 1,607 meters up in the mountains yet almost never freezes, because its water is slightly salty; its name means hot lake in Kyrgyz.
funFact.note: 150 characters. Wikipedia: elevation 1,607 m, salinity about 0.6 percent, rarely freezes, name means hot lake.

driveSide.note: Listed as RHT; matches seed leftHand=false.

flag.text: Adopted in 1992 after Soviet rule ended, and redrawn by law in 2023 so the sun's rays were straight and looked less like a sunflower. Officially the red stands for bravery and recalls the banner of Manas, hero of the Kyrgyz national epic. The gold sun means peace and wealth, and its forty rays stand for the forty tribes Manas united in legend. The red lines inside it show a tunduk, the round crown of a yurt roof, a symbol of hearth and home.

reasons.why: Adopted 3 March 1992, one day after Kyrgyzstan joined the United Nations. The amending law passed parliament on 20 December 2023, was signed on 22 December and came into force on 26 December 2023 (checked on Wikipedia). It straightened the previously wavy rays and increased the yurt beams of the tunduk from three to four, because the old sun was said to resemble a sunflower, which in Kyrgyz culture can mean a fickle and servile person.
Officially red stands for bravery and valor and alludes to the banner said to have been raised by Manas, the hero of the Kyrgyz epic.
Officially the sun epitomizes peace and prosperity.

Officially the forty rays stand for the number of tribes united by Manas to fight the Mongols, and also the number of his followers (Wikipedia, checked). Flags of the World phrases it as forty warriors of Manas. The name Kyrgyz is itself often read as forty tribes.

The crossed lines are a stylized tunduk, the roof opening of a traditional Kyrgyz yurt seen from inside; officially it represents the origin of life, the unity of time and space, and the people's hearth and home and their history.

entries.remainingDoubts: Population is the WPP 2024 mid-2024 value as reproduced by Worldometers (UN data portal returned 401). The official meanings come from Wikipedia and Flags of the World quoting the flag law; the law text itself on a government site was not opened. Sources differ on whether the forty rays mean forty tribes, forty followers or forty warriors of Manas. Burana Tower not separately verified.

currency.note: ISO code TJS; the common abbreviation SM is not a standard symbol.

landmarks.note: The Pamir range was confirmed via the Ismoil Somoni Peak page. Iskanderkul (mountain lake in the Fann Mountains) and Hisor Fortress (near Dushanbe) are well known but were not separately verified.

funFact.value: Mountains cover over 90 percent of Tajikistan; Ismoil Somoni Peak in the Pamirs, at 7,495 meters, was the highest point in the former Soviet Union.
funFact.note: 147 characters. Wikipedia: mountains cover more than 90 percent of the country; peak height 7,495 m, highest in Tajikistan and the former USSR.

driveSide.note: Listed as RHT; matches seed leftHand=false.

flag.text: Adopted in 1992 after Soviet rule ended. The bands keep the red, white and green of the Soviet-era Tajik flag, with a wider white band. Officially red means national unity, white means cotton and mountain snow, and green means fertile valleys. The crown is often read as a sign of the Tajik people, whose name is popularly linked to the Persian word for crown. Seven stars sit above it: seven means perfection and happiness in Persian tradition.

reasons.why: Adopted 24 November 1992 (checked on Wikipedia), replacing the flag of the Soviet Tajik republic approved in 1953.

reasons.feature: Three bands of red, white and green, white band wider (2:3:2)
reasons.why: The colors and the wider white middle band are kept from the 1953 Soviet-era Tajik flag, which also had red, white and green stripes with the white wider than the green. Wikipedia, citing the Embassy of Tajikistan's statement on state symbols, gives the official meanings: red is the color of the unification of the republic and brotherhood with other nations (also given as unity of the nation, victory and sunrise); white is the republic's main wealth, cotton, and the snow and ice of the high mountains; green stands for the valleys and nature (also fertile valleys, Islam and Novruz).

Wikipedia (checked) says the crown represents the Tajik people and the medieval Samanid dynasty, noting that the name Tajik is connected in popular etymology with the Persian word taj, meaning crown. Flags of the World reports an official reading of the crown and stars as sovereignty and friendship between nationalities. Because no law text giving the meaning was found, it is labeled traditional.

reasons.feature: Seven gold stars in an arc
reasons.why: Wikipedia (checked): the number seven is a symbol of perfection and happiness in Persian tradition, following a belief that the heavens hold seven mountains and seven orchard gardens with a star shining above each mountain. Some sources also link the stars to seven historical regions. No single meaning is fixed in law as far as the opened sources show.

entries.remainingDoubts: Population is the WPP 2024 mid-2024 value as reproduced by Worldometers (UN data portal returned 401). The flag's official regulation text was not found on a government site; color meanings follow Wikipedia's quotation of the Embassy of Tajikistan and secondary sources, and the crown and star meanings are labeled traditional because sources disagree (people/crown etymology and Samanids vs sovereignty vs seven regions). Russian is constitutionally the language of interethnic communication, not official, so only Tajik is listed. Iskanderkul and Hisor Fortress not separately verified. Area: the Wikipedia list total (144,100) differs from the country article infobox (143,100); the list value is used per the rules.

entries.name: Turkmenistan

officialName.note: The state's full name is simply Turkmenistan (Türkmenistan); the Wikipedia infobox and UN member list use no longer form.

capital.note: Single capital, confirmed in the Wikipedia infobox.

population.note: UN WPP 2024 revision, medium variant, 1 July 2024 estimate 7,494,498 (read via Worldometers' table, which cites WPP 2024; the UN data portal API returned 401). Rounded to 3 significant figures. Verification pass: the Wikipedia UN list (WPP 2024) only shows 1 July 2022 = 7,230,193 and 1 July 2023 = 7,364,438, so the 2024 figure could not be cross-checked there, but it is consistent with that growth trend.

areaSqKm.note: Total area per Wikipedia's list of countries by area: 469,930 km2 land plus 18,170 km2 inland water (rank 51). The country article's infobox gives 491,210 km2 instead.

languages.note: Turkmen is the sole official (state) language per the Wikipedia infobox; Russian is widely used but not official and is omitted.

currency.note: Infobox lists the manat, ISO code TMT; the local symbol is a lowercase m, so the ISO code is used.

landmarks.note: Merv and Kunya-Urgench are UNESCO World Heritage Sites named in the Wikipedia article; the Darvaza crater is the country's best-known sight, though the government has discussed extinguishing it and its flames have reportedly weakened, so it may need review in future.

funFact.value: The Karakum Desert covers most of Turkmenistan, and in 1995 the United Nations recognized the country as a permanently neutral state.
funFact.note: 133 characters. Wikipedia says the Karakum covers over 80 percent of the country; the UN neutrality recognition (12 December 1995) is confirmed in the flag article.

driveSide.note: Wikipedia infobox: drives on the right (seed leftHand=false agrees). The Left- and right-hand traffic list page was truncated when fetched so it could not be double-checked there.

flag.text: Adopted in 1992, the flag is described by law as a symbol of national unity, independence and neutrality. The red stripe shows five carpet patterns, each said to stand for one of the main Turkmen tribes and their famous weaving. Olive branches were added in 1997 after the United Nations recognized the country as permanently neutral. No official meaning is given for the green, crescent or five stars, often said to be the five provinces.

reasons.feature: Adoption in 1992 and the law's stated meaning
reasons.why: Adopted 19 February 1992 after independence from the Soviet Union (confirmed in the Wikipedia flag article; the current 2:3 version dates from 24 January 2001); the amended flag law states the flag is a symbol of the unity and independence of the nation and the neutrality of the state.

reasons.feature: Red vertical stripe with five carpet guls
reasons.why: The five guls are traditional carpet patterns associated with the five major Turkmen tribes (Teke, Yomut, Saryk, Chowdur, Ersari per Wikipedia, confirmed on this pass; Britannica and the 2003 emblem text give slightly different tribe lists), reflecting the country's carpet-weaving heritage. The law itself does not name tribes, so hedged as 'said to'.

reasons.feature: Two crossed olive branches below the guls
reasons.why: Added by law on 29 January 1997 after the UN General Assembly recognized Turkmenistan's permanent neutrality on 12 December 1995 (both dates confirmed in the Wikipedia flag article); the decree says they mark the peace-loving nature of the people and the state's neutral status, echoing the UN flag.

Wikipedia states that no official explanation has been given for the flag's colors; the Russian Centre of Vexillology and Heraldry reads green as life, land, grass, prosperity and peace, and Britannica as a reference to Islam.

No official meaning is given (Wikipedia: no official explanation for the white symbols). The stars are popularly said to stand for the five provinces (Ahal, Balkan, Dashoguz, Lebap, Mary), sometimes also the Five Pillars of Islam; 1992 newspapers made them the five senses, and the crescent is read as hope for a bright future or a clear sky.

entries.remainingDoubts: Population comes from Worldometers' reproduction of the WPP 2024 table rather than the UN portal itself (UN API needed authentication); the Wikipedia UN list only carries 2022 and 2023 columns, so the mid-2024 figure is unverified against a UN page. The law's wording (unity, independence, neutrality) was not re-opened in the law text on this pass and rests on the Wikipedia and FOTW renderings. Area differs between Wikipedia's area list (488,100) and the country infobox (491,210); the list value was used as instructed. Tribe lists for the five guls vary by source, so the text keeps them unnamed. flagColors are ordered hoist to fly, which puts the red stripe before the dominant green. Darvaza crater's long-term future is uncertain.

landmarks.note: Registan, the historic centre of Bukhara and Itchan Kala are named in the Wikipedia article; the Kalyan Minaret is chosen as Bukhara's best-known single monument.

funFact.value: Uzbekistan is one of only two doubly landlocked countries on Earth, meaning all of its neighbors are landlocked too; the other is Liechtenstein.
funFact.note: 144 characters. Stated in the Wikipedia lead.

flag.text: Adopted in 1991 as Uzbekistan left the Soviet Union, the flag came from a design contest. The government says blue stands for the sky and water, white for peace and good luck, green for nature and new life, and the thin red stripes for the power of life. The crescent marks the newly independent republic. The twelve stars officially recall the people's history and an ancient solar calendar; many also link them to the region's astronomers.

reasons.feature: Adoption in 1991 after a design contest
reasons.why: Adopted 18 November 1991 by the Supreme Soviet of the newly independent republic (date confirmed on the government's state-symbols page), chosen from over 200 competition entries; the winning design is credited to Farhod Yoʻldoshev.

The government's state-symbols page says blue is 'the symbol of the sky and water, which are the main source of life' (confirmed on this pass). Britannica adds a traditional link to the banner of the 14th-century ruler Timur, left out of the text for length.
Official page: 'the traditional symbol of peace and good luck' (Britannica adds moral purity).
Official page: 'the color of nature and new life and good harvest'.
Official page: 'Two thin red stripes symbolize the power of life.'
Official page: the new moon 'symbolizes the newly independent Republic'; sources note it is read as independence rather than as a religious symbol, though Britannica also mentions Muslim symbolism.

reasons.feature: Twelve white stars in rows of 3, 4 and 5
reasons.why: Official page: the twelve stars 'stand for spiritual sign' and refer to 'the historical traditions of the Uzbek people, as well as ancient solar calendar' and the ancient roots of local culture. The link to the region's astronomy (medieval Samarkand) and readings as the twelve regions, months or zodiac signs are popular glosses from Britannica and FOTW, so the text hedges them. Wikipedia notes the flag law itself gives construction details only, not meanings.

entries.remainingDoubts: The color meanings come from the government's state-symbols web page (re-read on this pass) rather than the flag law (Law No. 407-XII), which only specifies construction; Wikipedia therefore calls the symbolism not officially designated, so 'official' here means stated by the government portal. The astronomy reading of the twelve stars is a popular gloss and is hedged in the text. Population taken from Worldometers' copy of the WPP 2024 table (UN API needed authentication; the Wikipedia UN list only carries 2022 and 2023 columns). Area list value (447,400) differs from the country infobox (448,978). Karakalpak omitted as regional-only; include it if the app wants co-official regional languages.

capital.note: Owner rule: capital Ulaanbaatar. Matches the Wikipedia infobox.

population.note: UN World Population Prospects 2024, mid-2024 medium variant: 3,475,540, rounded to 3 significant figures. The UN data portal API returned HTTP 401, so the figure was read from Worldometers' table, which states it is WPP 2024 data; Wikipedia's UN list only showed the 2023 column (3,431,932) and is consistent. Not re-verified at the UN source in the review pass.

areaSqKm.note: Total area per Wikipedia's list: land 1,557,507 km2 plus inland water 6,609 km2.

languages.note: Article 8 of the constitution, read at constituteproject.org: the Mongolian language shall be the official language of the State.

currency.note: ISO code MNT; sole legal tender since 1928.

landmarks.note: Gobi Desert is shared with China but its Mongolian part is the country's best-known landscape. The 40 m statue (opened 2008) stands 54 km east of Ulaanbaatar; Erdene Zuu (founded 1585) is inside the Orkhon Valley World Heritage Site.

funFact.value: Mongolia is the world's most sparsely populated country, and many families still live as nomadic herders in round felt tents called gers.
funFact.note: 137 characters. Wikipedia: most sparsely populated sovereign state (about 2.2 people per km2) and roughly 30 percent of the population nomadic or semi-nomadic; the density gap to the next country is large, so the statement should hold.

driveSide.note: Seed leftHand=false; WorldStandards lists Mongolia as driving on the right. No source disagrees.

flag.text: Mongolia's flag has three bands, red, blue and red. The 1992 constitution says blue is the eternal blue sky, red stands for progress and prosperity, and the golden Soyombo by the pole expresses independence, sovereignty and spirit. The monk Zanabazar designed the Soyombo in 1686; its flame, sun, moon, arrow points, bars and two fish are often read as growth, lasting life, courage, honesty and vigilance.

reasons.why: Article 12 of the 1992 constitution says the blue middle third of the flag symbolizes the eternal blue sky.
Article 12 of the constitution says the red bands on both sides symbolize progress and prosperity.

reasons.feature: Golden Soyombo near the pole (official meaning)
reasons.why: Article 12 of the constitution places the golden Soyombo on the red band nearest the pole and says it signifies Mongolia's independence, sovereignty and spirit.

The Soyombo is a national symbol created by the Buddhist monk and artist Zanabazar in 1686 as the first character of his Soyombo script; it has been on Mongolian flags since independence from the Qing in 1911 and in its present form since 1945.

reasons.feature: Soyombo elements: flame, sun, moon, triangles, bars, yin-yang fish, side walls
reasons.why: Commonly given readings: the three-tongued flame is growth and past, present and future; sun and moon the nation's eternal existence; the two triangles arrow or spear points against enemies; the horizontal bars honesty and justice; the yin-yang is two fish that never close their eyes, for vigilance; the vertical rectangles are fortress walls for unity. No law fixes these meanings, so the text says they are often read this way.
The constitution only specifies that the Soyombo is golden; Wikipedia's uncited claim that yellow stands for Tibetan Buddhism is not backed by law, so no official meaning is given.

reasons.feature: No star above the Soyombo (change of 1992)
reasons.why: A five-pointed star placed above the Soyombo in the communist era was removed on 12 February 1992 when the democratic constitution took effect (the constitution's own effective date, read at constituteproject.org). Not mentioned in the text to keep it under 420 characters.

entries.remainingDoubts: Population was read from Worldometers' reproduction of WPP 2024 (3,475,540) because the UN data portal API refused the request; confirm against the UN file if strictness matters. Soyombo element meanings are traditional, not in law; the constitution's own meaning for the Soyombo (independence, sovereignty and spirit) is now in the text. Flag text is about 406 characters.

entries.name: North Korea

officialName.note: Owner rule and Wikipedia infobox agree.

capital.note: Owner rule: capital Pyongyang.

sources: population rounding rule in the task brief (no page opened; value unchanged from the entry's own WPP 2024 figure 26,498,823)
population.note: critic: Inconsistent rounding across the batch's edge cases: KP went to 5 significant figures (26,499,000) while MM (54,500,000) and PS (5,495,000) stopped at the rule's 3-or-4 figures even though the result still ends in 5 and zeros. The rule as written is 3 s.f., 4 if the third digit is 5; 26,498,823 gives 26,500,000 either way. Apply the literal rule for all three; if the no-trailing-5 clause is instead enforced by a validator, keep 26,499,000 and change MM to 54,500,100 and PS to 5,495,400. Hand edit: stored at 5 significant figures (WPP 26,498,823) because 26,500,000 would sit on a compact-rounding tie.

areaSqKm.note: Total area per Wikipedia's list: land 120,410 km2 plus inland water 130 km2 (figures rounded in the source, so land plus water is 2 km2 off the total).

languages.note: Official language Korean (the Pyongyang-based Munhwaŏ standard).

currency.note: ISO code KPW; Wikipedia titles the article North Korean won and calls it formally the Korean people's won.

landmarks.note: Juche Tower is a 170 m monument completed in 1982; the Arch of Triumph is modeled on, and larger than, the Paris arch. Mount Paektu straddles the border with China; its highest point (Janggun Peak) is on the North Korean side.

funFact.value: Mount Paektu, a volcano on the border with China, is the highest peak of the Korean Peninsula and holds a deep crater lake called Heaven Lake.
funFact.note: 142 characters. 2,744 m, active stratovolcano (last eruption 1903), crater lake Heaven Lake (Chonji) feeding the Yalu, Tumen and Songhua rivers; chosen as a neutral, durable fact.

driveSide.note: Seed leftHand=false; right-hand traffic since 1946. No source disagrees.

flag.text: North Korea adopted this flag on 8 September 1948 with its first constitution, replacing the old Korean flag with the red and blue swirl. The state says the wide red band is the blood of patriots who fought Japanese rule, the white stripes are one people with one land, language and culture, and the blue stripes are the people's spirit for world peace. The red star in a white circle is called the symbol of socialism. Its designer is disputed.

reasons.why: State newspaper Rodong Sinmun (8 August 2013), as quoted by Wikipedia, says the red band symbolizes the anti-Japanese fervor and the red blood shed by Korean patriots; the CIA World Factbook summarizes red as revolutionary traditions.
Rodong Sinmun says the white stripes symbolize one bloodline, one land, one language and one culture of a single people; the Factbook gives purity, strength and dignity.
Rodong Sinmun says the blue stripes stand for the gallant visage of the people, symbolizing the spirit fighting for world peace; the Factbook gives sovereignty, peace and friendship.

reasons.feature: Red five-pointed star in a white disc
reasons.why: The red star is described as the symbol of socialism (CIA World Factbook summary of the state's meaning, via Wikipedia); the state account says Kim Il Sung ordered the star added and the disc moved toward the pole in February 1948. The text says it is called the symbol of socialism rather than stating it as fact.

The flag replaced the taegukgi (the flag of Korea since 1883, with a centered red-and-blue swirl and four trigrams, still used by South Korea) when the first constitution of the DPRK was passed by the Supreme People's Assembly; it is described in the constitution (Wikipedia now cites Chapter VII, Article 166 after the 2026 revision) and the 1992 National Flag Law.

Attribution is disputed: the state credits Kim Il Sung, the artist Kim Chu-gyong was earlier recognized as designer, and Soviet-Korean witnesses (Pak Il, corroborated by Chong Sangjin) said the Soviet side produced the design. The text says only that the designer is disputed.

entries.remainingDoubts: Population: 26,498,823 rounds to 26,500,000 at both 3 and 4 significant figures, which ends in 5 followed by zeros, so 26,499,000 (5 s.f.) is returned; use 26,500,000 if the s.f. rule outranks the no-trailing-5 rule. The official color meanings come from state media and the constitution as quoted on Wikipedia, not read at source; the Rodong Sinmun quote for blue was seen only as far as world peace, so the earlier draft's and progress was dropped. Wikipedia reports that on 23 March 2026 the flag's proportions changed from 1:2 to 1:1.65 and the constitution's flag article moved to Article 166; the text avoids proportions and article numbers, but the stored flag image may show the older proportions. Mount Paektu straddles the China border. Flag text is about 447 characters, within the 450 limit but above the 420 aim.

languages.note: Mandarin Chinese is the de facto official language. The 2019 National Languages Development Act makes every native language and Taiwan Sign Language a national language (the Wikipedia infobox lists six); the catalog lists Mandarin alone, as it lists only state-wide languages for other countries. Mandarin is the official language de facto (no law names an official language). The 2019 National Languages Development Act makes every natural language of Taiwan's ethnic groups plus Taiwan Sign Language a national language; the Wikipedia infobox lists these six. Formosan languages is a family of indigenous languages, not one language. If a shorter list is wanted, Mandarin Chinese alone is defensible.

currency.note: Owner rule. ISO code TWD.

landmarks.note: All three are named among Taiwan's best-known sights in the Wikipedia article.

funFact.value: Taiwan has its own government, elections and currency, but its status is disputed: China claims it, and most countries do not recognize it as a state.
funFact.note: The agreed status sentence verbatim (150 characters), checked against the seed's ownerRules; it fills the 160-character budget so no second fact is added.

driveSide.note: Seed leftHand=false; left-hand traffic under Japanese rule 1895-1945, right-hand traffic since 1946. No source disagrees.

flag.text: The white sun on blue in the upper left corner was drawn by Lu Haodong in 1895 for Sun Yat-sen's revolutionary group. Sun added the red in 1906. It became the Kuomintang party emblem and, in 1928, the national flag of the Republic of China. The twelve rays mark the months and the twelve two-hour periods of a traditional day. Sun tied blue to liberty, white to equality and red to brotherhood and the blood of the revolutionaries.

reasons.feature: White sun on a blue rectangle in the upper left corner (Blue Sky with a White Sun)
reasons.why: Designed by Lu Haodong and presented on 21 February 1895 as the emblem of the Revive China Society (Society for Regenerating China) in Hong Kong, Sun Yat-sen's group working to overthrow the Qing dynasty; it later became the emblem of the Kuomintang party and remains in the party flag.
Stand for the twelve months of the year and the twelve traditional two-hour periods (shichen) of the day, a sign of constant progress.
Added by Sun Yat-sen in the winter of 1906 to complete the design; red is said to commemorate the blood of the revolutionaries who died for the cause.

Sun Yat-sen, who completed the design, explained the colors through his Three Principles of the People: blue for nationalism and liberty, white for democracy and equality, red for the people's livelihood and fraternity. Wikipedia presents this as the standard explanation attributed to the designer rather than citing a statute; the ROC government page giving the same meanings was not opened in this pass.

Used as the naval flag from 1912; made the national flag of the Republic of China by the National Emblem and National Flag Act on 17 December 1928 after the Kuomintang's Nationalist government completed the Northern Expedition; written into Article 6 of the 1947 constitution, which remains in force in Taiwan.

entries.remainingDoubts: Area: the Wikipedia list gives 35,980 km2 while the Taiwan article and ROC government give about 36,197 km2; the list figure is used per the rules. The six-language list follows the Wikipedia infobox reading of the 2019 National Languages Development Act; Mandarin's official status is only de facto. Population is listed by WPP under China, Taiwan Province of China and was read from Worldometers' reproduction of WPP 2024. The color meanings are Sun Yat-sen's own explanation as reported by Wikipedia; a government source stating them was not opened, so downgrade the basis to traditional if designer attribution is not accepted as official. Flag text (431 characters) omits the 1949 move to Taiwan to stay within length.

entries.name: Brunei

officialName.note: Seed ownerRules fix this form (Malay: Negara Brunei Darussalam, 'Nation of Brunei, the Abode of Peace'); Wikipedia infobox and the constitution's English text use 'Brunei Darussalam'.

capital.note: Single capital; matches seed ownerRules.

population.note: UN WPP 2024 revision, mid-2024 estimate 462,721 rounded to 3 s.f. Verification: the Wikipedia UN list (opened) confirms the WPP 2024 revision but shows only the 1 July 2022 and 1 July 2023 columns (455,370 and 458,949, +0.79%/yr); extrapolating one year gives about 462,600, which also rounds to 463,000. The exact 2024 figure is from recollection of WPP 2024 (population.un.org needs a token); the rounded value is robust.

areaSqKm.note: Total area 5,765 km2 = 5,270 km2 land + about 500 km2 inland water, per Wikipedia's list.

languages.note: Constitution Article 82: 'The official language of Brunei Darussalam shall be the Malay language.' English is widely used in law and schools but is not an official language.

currency.note: ISO BND. Under the 1967 Currency Interchangeability Agreement the Singapore dollar circulates at par as 'customary tender', not legal tender, so only one currency is listed.

value: Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddien Mosque (Bandar Seri Begawan)
landmarks.note: Mosque spelled 'Saifuddien' as in its Wikipedia title (the tourism article writes 'Saifuddin'). Kampong Ayer is the stilt water village on the Brunei River; Ulu Temburong is the main rainforest park in the eastern Temburong District.

funFact.value: Brunei is the only sovereign country lying entirely on the island of Borneo, and the Malaysian district of Limbang splits it into two separate parts.
funFact.note: 149 characters. Wikipedia lead: only sovereign state entirely on Borneo; territory bifurcated by Limbang (Sarawak, Malaysia).

driveSide.note: Left-hand traffic, inherited from British Borneo; matches seed leftHand=true.

flag.text: Until 1906 the flag was plain yellow, traditionally the sultan's color. White and black diagonal stripes were then added for his two chief ministers. The red emblem was added in 1959 with the constitution: the crescent stands for Islam, the umbrella for the monarchy, the wings for justice, peace and prosperity, and the hands for the government's care of its people. The Arabic writing gives the national motto and the country's name.

reasons.why: Brunei's flag was a plain yellow banner before 1906; yellow is the traditional royal color of Southeast Asia and is read as standing for the sultan and the monarchy (Wikipedia: 'in Southeast Asia, yellow is traditionally the colour of royalty').

Added in 1906 when Brunei signed its treaty with Britain; white (the slightly wider stripe, about 12% wider per Wikipedia) for the Pengiran Bendahara (first minister) and black for the Pengiran Pemancha (second minister), the two wazirs who signed alongside the sultan. FOTW notes an official 1999 booklet gives no color symbolism, so this is documented history rather than a current legal meaning.

The national emblem was placed on the flag on 29 September 1959, when the first written constitution was proclaimed (Wikipedia infobox: adopted 29 September 1959); red is said to stand for bravery and unity.
Symbol of Islam, the state religion.

reasons.feature: Royal umbrella and small flag at the top
reasons.why: Items of the sultan's regalia, standing for the monarchy.
Stated to symbolize the protection of justice, tranquility, prosperity and peace.
Stated to show the government's duty to preserve and promote the welfare of the people (Wikipedia: 'government benevolence').

On the crescent: the national motto, 'Always render service with God's guidance' (Malay: Sentiasa Membuat Kebajikan Dengan Petunjuk Allah); on the ribbon below: 'Brunei Darussalam', the country's name.

entries.remainingDoubts: Mid-2024 WPP figure (462,721) not opened directly; the opened Wikipedia UN list shows only the 2022 and 2023 columns, but the +0.79% growth extrapolation also rounds to 463,000. No gov.bn page or law stating color meanings was found; the Flag of Brunei article cites no statute for them, so the crest meanings rest on Wikipedia/FOTW quoting Information Department publications. Mosque landmark spelling follows the Wikipedia title ('Saifuddien').

officialName.note: Infobox and constitution title.

population.note: UN WPP 2024 revision, mid-2024 estimate 17,638,801 rounded to 3 s.f. Verification: the Wikipedia UN list (opened) confirms the WPP 2024 revision but shows only the 1 July 2022 and 1 July 2023 columns (17,201,724 and 17,423,880, +1.29%/yr); extrapolating one year gives about 17.65 million, which also rounds to 17,600,000. The exact 2024 figure is from recollection of WPP 2024; the rounded value is robust.

areaSqKm.note: Total area 181,035 km2 = 176,520 km2 land + 4,520 km2 inland water (Tonle Sap and rivers), per Wikipedia's list.

languages.note: Constitution Article 5: 'The official language and script is Khmer.'

currency.note: ISO KHR. The US dollar is very widely used in daily life, but the riel is the national currency and the only one issued by the state, so one currency is listed.

landmarks.note: Angkor Wat is the largest religious monument in the world; Bayon is the face-tower temple of Angkor Thom; the Royal Palace is the king's residence in the capital.

funFact.value: Each rainy season the Tonlé Sap river reverses its flow, and the Mekong's floodwater swells Tonlé Sap lake to several times its dry-season size.
funFact.note: 144 characters. Tonle Sap article: the river flows from the Mekong into the lake May to October and back November to April; the lake grows from roughly 2,500-3,000 km2 to about 16,000 km2 (Cambodia article gives up to 24,605 km2), so 'several times' is safe.

driveSide.note: Right-hand traffic since French Indochina; right-hand-drive cars were banned in 2001. Matches seed leftHand=false.

flag.text: Cambodian flags have shown Angkor Wat, the 12th-century Khmer Empire temple, since about 1875. The present design, a wide red band between two blue ones with the temple in white, was adopted in 1948 and brought back in 1993 when the monarchy was restored. The colors are often linked to the national motto Nation, Religion, King, with red read as the nation, white as religion and blue as the king.

reasons.feature: White Angkor Wat temple in the center
reasons.why: Khmer flags have carried Angkor Wat, the 12th-century temple of the Khmer Empire and the symbol of national heritage, since around 1875 under the French protectorate (Wikipedia: 'Since around 1875, the Cambodian flag has featured a depiction of Angkor Wat in the centre'); the 1948 version redrew it closer to the real building. On the current flag (image checked) the temple is drawn from the front in white with black outlines, showing three towers on a stepped base. Cambodia is one of very few countries with a building on its flag.

reasons.feature: Blue, red, blue horizontal bands with the red band twice as wide
reasons.why: Ratio 1:2:1 blue-red-blue. This layout was adopted in 1948 (Wikipedia infobox: 1948 to 9 October 1970), replaced by other designs from 1970 to 1993 (Khmer Republic, Khmer Rouge, People's Republic, UNTAC), and readopted on 24 September 1993 with the constitution when the monarchy returned; the constitution (Article 6) defines the flag in its Annex 1. Wikipedia adds that 'red and blue are traditionally the colours of Cambodia'.

Popularly tied to the constitutional motto 'Nation, Religion, King' (Article 4): red for the nation (bravery), white for religion (integrity, justice, heritage) and blue for the king (liberty, cooperation, brotherhood). The Flag of Cambodia article gives this table without citing a law, Britannica gives no color meaning, and the constitutional annex could not be opened, so it is presented as a common reading.

entries.remainingDoubts: Mid-2024 WPP figure (17,638,801) not opened directly; the opened Wikipedia UN list shows only the 2022 and 2023 columns, but the +1.29% extrapolation also rounds to 17,600,000. Readoption date differs by source: Wikipedia gives 24 September 1993 (constitution), Britannica says the 1948 flag was hoisted again on 30 June 1993; the text says only 'in 1993'. The constitution's Annex 1 text on the flag was not shown on constituteproject, so whether it states color meanings is unverified (treated as traditional). The three-tower rendering is taken from the flag image itself, not from a text source.

entries.name: Indonesia

officialName.note: Infobox; Indonesian: Republik Indonesia.

capital.note: Seed ownerRules are binding: Jakarta. Law 3/2022 designates Nusantara (East Kalimantan) as the future capital, but the Wikipedia infobox still lists Jakarta and the Nusantara article describes the move as planned and gradual rather than completed; no dated wording used.

population.note: UN WPP 2024 revision, mid-2024 estimate 283,487,931 rounded to 3 s.f. Verification: the Wikipedia UN list (opened) confirms the WPP 2024 revision but shows only the 1 July 2022 and 1 July 2023 columns (278,830,529 and 281,190,067, +0.85%/yr). A flat extrapolation of that rate gives about 283.6 million (which would round to 284,000,000), but growth is slowing and the WPP 2024 mid-2024 figure as I recall it is 283,487,931, which rounds to 283,000,000. The exact figure was not opened; see remainingDoubts.

areaSqKm.note: Total area 1,904,569 km2 = 1,811,569 km2 land + 93,000 km2 inland water, per Wikipedia's list (footnote [s] on the source); excludes the sea between the islands.

languages.note: Indonesian (Bahasa Indonesia) is the sole official language under the 1945 Constitution (Article 36) and Law 24/2009; hundreds of regional languages such as Javanese are not official nationally.

currency.note: ISO IDR.

landmarks.note: Borobudur is the giant 9th-century Buddhist monument in Central Java; Komodo National Park holds the largest Komodo dragon populations; Mount Bromo is the famous active volcano in East Java. Prambanan, Lake Toba and Raja Ampat are good alternates.

funFact.value: The Komodo dragon, the largest living lizard, lives in the wild only on a few Indonesian islands such as Komodo, Rinca and Flores.
funFact.note: 130 characters. Komodo dragon article: largest extant lizard; native to Komodo, Rinca, Flores, Gili Motang and Gili Dasami (extinct on Padar since 1975).

driveSide.note: Left-hand road traffic (trains run on the right, unusually). Matches seed leftHand=true.

flag.text: Indonesia's flag, two equal bands, red over white, is called Sang Saka Merah-Putih, the Heirloom Red and White. The colors go back to the banners of the 13th-century Majapahit Empire, and nationalists revived them in the 1920s under Dutch rule. The flag was raised at the declaration of independence on 17 August 1945 and is named in the constitution. Red is said to stand for courage and white for purity; some also pair them as body and soul.

reasons.why: The red and white pairing is traced to the banners of the Majapahit Empire (founded 1293 in Java); the Pararaton chronicle describes a red and white banner used by Jayakatwang's troops against Singhasari even earlier. The design appeared on the cover of the Perhimpoenan Indonesia magazine (1908-1923), Indonesian nationalist students adopted the red-white flag in 1922, and Wikipedia records the modern flag first flown in Java in 1928 under Dutch rule.

Introduced and hoisted in public at the proclamation of independence on 17 August 1945 in Jakarta (the flag sewn by Fatmawati is the 'heirloom' Bendera Pusaka, too fragile for use after 1968); Article 35 of the 1945 Constitution names the national flag Sang Saka Merah-Putih (The Heirloom Red-White), and Government Regulation 40/1958 and Law 24/2009 regulate its 2:3 design and use.

Red is said to stand for courage and white for purity, words used by first president Sukarno ('Red is the symbol of courage, White is the symbol of purity'); another common reading pairs red with the body or physical life and white with the soul, together making a whole person. Britannica gives the Majapahit tradition as red for courage and white for honesty. The Flag of Indonesia article does not attribute these meanings to Law 24/2009 or Article 35, so they are presented as 'said to'.

entries.remainingDoubts: Mid-2024 WPP figure (283,487,931) not opened directly; the opened Wikipedia UN list shows only the 2022 and 2023 columns, and a flat +0.85% extrapolation would give about 283.6 million (rounding to 284,000,000), so the 283,000,000 value depends on the recalled WPP 2024 figure; confirm at population.un.org before shipping. Whether Law 24/2009 itself states the color meanings is unverified (Wikipedia and the hukumonline summary do not attribute them to the law), so the meaning is labeled traditional. Capital follows the owner rule (Jakarta); the Nusantara article hints at later changes to Jakarta's special status without giving the legal instrument, so re-check before any future batch touches this entry. The Monaco look-alike fact was left out of the flag text for length.

flag.text: Lao scholar Maha Sila Viravong designed the flag in 1945 for the Lao Issara independence movement. It became the national flag in 1975, when the monarchy ended and its red flag with a white three-headed elephant was dropped. Red is officially said to stand for blood shed in the fight for freedom, blue for the Mekong River and the nation's wealth, and the white disc for a full moon over the Mekong and the unity of the Lao people.

reasons.why: Designed in 1945 by Maha Sila Viravong and selected by the Lao Issara government on 12 October 1945, deliberately unlike the royal red flag with a white three-headed elephant; readopted 2 December 1975 when the Lao PDR was proclaimed. Constitution Article 112 describes it as dark blue with red edges and a white moon in the middle. Verified against the Flag of Laos article (image checked: red-blue-red bands with a white disc).
Blood shed by the Lao people in the struggle for freedom and independence, per the designer's account quoted in the Flag of Laos article and the official reading quoted by FOTW.
The Mekong River, a symbol of the nation's prosperity, per the designer's account and the official reading.

The designer said it stands for the unity of the Lao people; it is also described as a full moon over the Mekong, and the constitution calls it a white moon. Other readings (unity under the ruling party, a bright future) circulate in flag books but are not the designer's wording.

entries.remainingDoubts: Population comes from Worldometers' mirror of WPP 2024 (7,769,819 for 2024), not the UN data portal itself. The area list's footnote [aw] was not read. Constitution article numbers (110, 112, 116) come from the draft and were not re-opened in the verification pass. The designer's meanings for the flag come via Wikipedia and FOTW quoting Maha Sila Viravong; no Lao government text stating the color meanings was found beyond the constitution's physical description.

population.note: UN WPP 2024 revision, mid-2024 medium variant: 35,557,673, rounded to 3 significant figures (35.6 million). Read from Worldometers' WPP 2024 mirror; the Wikipedia UN list only showed the 1 July 2023 column (35,126,298). The national statistics department's own series is lower and is not used.

areaSqKm.note: Total per Wikipedia's area list: 329,432 km2 land plus 1,190 km2 water (list total 330,621). The Malaysia country article's infobox gives 330,803 km2 instead; the list figure is used as the rules require.

languages.note: Infobox: Malaysian Malay is the national language (official, Constitution Article 152). English has official uses in some states and courts but is not an official language nationwide, so it is omitted. The constitution text itself was not opened.

currency.note: ISO code MYR; symbol RM per the Wikipedia infobox.

landmarks.note: All three are well-known sights inside Malaysia; Mount Kinabalu is in Sabah on Borneo.

funFact.value: Malaysia is split in two by the South China Sea: Peninsular Malaysia on the Asian mainland and the states of Sabah and Sarawak on the island of Borneo.
funFact.note: Stated in the Wikipedia Malaysia article (two regions separated by the South China Sea); 151 characters.

driveSide.note: Matches the seed (leftHand true). Left-hand traffic introduced under British rule and retained.

flag.text: Mohamed Hamzah's design won a 1949 contest and flew from 1950 with 11 stripes and an 11-point star for Malaya's 11 states; three were added when Malaysia formed in 1963. Officially the 14 stripes and 14 star points stand for the equal status of the 13 states and the federal government, the crescent for Islam, yellow for the royal color of the Malay rulers, blue for the unity of the people, red for bravery and white for purity.

reasons.why: Chosen through a 1949 Federal Legislative Council competition (373 entries) won by Johor architect Mohamed Hamzah, aged 29; approved 19 May 1950 and first raised 26 May 1950 for the Federation of Malaya with 11 stripes and an 11-point star for the 11 states, then changed on 16 September 1963 to 14 stripes and points when Sabah, Sarawak and Singapore joined. The 14 were kept after Singapore left in 1965. Named Jalur Gemilang (Stripes of Glory) in 1997. Image checked: blue upper-left rectangle with yellow crescent and 14-point star, 14 red and white stripes.

Equal status in the federation of the member states and the federal government (13 states plus the federal government, per the official Malaysian Year Book quoted by FOTW). The Flag of Malaysia Wikipedia article instead phrases the 14th as the federal territories; both readings are presented as official.
Unity of the 13 states with the federal government, per the official yearbook quoted by FOTW and the government portal cited by Wikipedia (the 14 points represent the unity among these entities).
Islam, the official religion of the federation.
The royal color of the Malay Rulers.
Unity of the Malaysian people.

Verified in the Flag of Malaysia Wikipedia article (citing the government account): the red stripes represent bravery and the white stripes purity; it adds that red, white and blue together also symbolise Malaysia's inclusion within the Commonwealth. The yearbook quote on FOTW does not give separate meanings for red and white.

entries.remainingDoubts: The official malaysia.gov.my flag page returned 404 in the drafting pass, so the official meanings rest on Wikipedia's citation of it and on an official yearbook quoted by FOTW; the two differ on whether the 14th stripe is the federal government or the federal territories (the text uses federal government, the yearbook wording). Area differs between the Wikipedia list (330,621) and the country article (330,803). Population is from Worldometers' mirror of WPP 2024, not the UN portal directly.

officialName.value: Republic of the Union of Myanmar
officialName.note: Per ownerRules; matches the Wikipedia infobox.

funFact.value: The ancient city of Bagan holds the remains of more than 2,000 Buddhist temples and pagodas built mainly between the 11th and 13th centuries.
funFact.note: Wikipedia (citing Stadtner 2011) says over 2,300 temples and pagodas survive from more than 10,000 built in the 11th to 13th centuries; 'more than 2,000' is a safe floor. 141 characters.

flag.text: Adopted in 2010 under a Union Flag Law based on the 2008 constitution, this flag replaced the 1974 red flag with 14 small stars in its upper left corner. Its three bands repeat the yellow, green and red of a flag Burma used in the 1940s. By law, yellow stands for unity and wisdom, green for peace, fairness and a green land, red for bravery and decisiveness, and the white star for purity, honesty, compassion and strength.

reasons.why: State Peace and Development Council Law No. 8/2010 (Union Flag Law), enacted 21 October 2010 to implement the flag described in the 2008 constitution; it replaced the 1974 flag (red with a blue upper-left corner holding 14 white stars for the administrative divisions). Verified on the WIPO Lex copy of the law. Image checked: yellow, green and red bands with a large white five-pointed star in the center.

The layout repeats the yellow-green-red flag used by the State of Burma in 1943-45; the Flag of Myanmar Wikipedia article links the colors to the flags of the independence period. The flag law itself does not state this origin, so the text keeps to the documented 1940s precedent.
Section 5 of the Union Flag Law: unity, conformity, huge wisdom, happiness and the amicable unity of all national races (verified on WIPO Lex).
Section 5 of the Union Flag Law: fertility, conformity, fairness and being a peaceful, pleasant and greening nation (verified on WIPO Lex).
Section 5 of the Union Flag Law: bravery and decisiveness (verified on WIPO Lex).
Section 5 of the Union Flag Law: purity, honesty, fullness of compassion and power (verified on WIPO Lex).

entries.remainingDoubts: The mid-2024 WPP figure (54,500,091) rounds to 54,500,000 at any reasonable precision, which the rule on values ending in 5 cannot avoid. Population is from Worldometers' mirror of WPP 2024, not the UN portal directly. Burmese's official status is taken from the Wikipedia infobox rather than the constitution text. The link between the bands and the 1940s flag is Wikipedia's statement, not wording in the flag law; the 1943-45 State of Burma was set up under Japanese occupation, so the text avoids calling it an independence flag.

landmarks.note: Wikipedia summaries confirm the terraces in Ifugao, the hills in Bohol province and Mayon, an active volcano in Albay.

funFact.value: The Philippines is an archipelago of more than 7,000 islands, grouped into three main regions: Luzon, the Visayas and Mindanao.
funFact.note: Wikipedia gives about 7,641 islands and the three main geographical divisions; 'more than 7,000' is stable wording. 127 characters.

driveSide.note: Right-hand traffic, formalized in 1945 by a decree of President Sergio Osmeña. Agrees with the seed (leftHand false).

flag.text: The flag was sewn in Hong Kong and unfurled when independence from Spain was declared in June 1898. The white triangle recalls the Katipunan secret society and officially means liberty, equality and brotherhood. The eight sun rays are the first eight provinces that rose against Spain, the three stars are Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao, blue means peace, truth and justice, and red means patriotism and courage. In war it is flown red side up.

reasons.why: Designed by Emilio Aguinaldo and sewn in Hong Kong by Marcela Agoncillo, her daughter Lorenza and Delfina Herbosa Natividad; first displayed in battle on 28 May 1898 and formally unfurled at the declaration of independence in Kawit on 12 June 1898. Confirmed on the Wikipedia flag article.

Inherited from the triangle used on the flags of the Katipunan, the secret society that started the 1896 revolution (itself linked to Masonic symbolism); the 1898 proclamation says the triangle is the Katipunan emblem. The current official explanation (as given on the Wikipedia flag article) is liberty, equality and fraternity, rendered as 'brotherhood' for young readers.

The 1898 Proclamation of Independence and the current official explanation give the eight rays as the first eight provinces that rose in revolt against Spain in 1896; the sun as a whole is explained as unity, freedom, people's democracy and sovereignty. The Wikipedia flag article lists Bulacan, Cavite, Pampanga, Laguna, Batangas, Tarlac, Nueva Ecija and the district of Morong; other versions name Manila or Bataan in place of Tarlac or Morong.
The three main island groups Luzon, Visayas and Mindanao (the 1898 proclamation named Luzon, Mindanao and Panay).

reasons.feature: Blue upper band and red lower band
reasons.why: The current official explanation: blue for peace, truth and justice; red for patriotism and valor (rendered as 'courage'). The 1898 proclamation instead said the blue, red and white commemorated the flag of the United States in gratitude for its help.
Republic Act 8491 (1998), Section 10: the flag has the blue field on top in time of peace and the red field on top in time of war; the Wikipedia flag article repeats the rule.

entries.remainingDoubts: Population is the WPP 2024 figure as reproduced by Worldometers, not read from population.un.org (API returned 401). The Official Gazette page on the flag (officialgazette.gov.ph) returned 403 earlier and was not retried, so the current official meanings of the colors, sun and stars rest on the Wikipedia flag article (re-read in this pass) and Britannica; the text of RA 8491 on Lawphil describes the design and the wartime rule but does not itself spell out the meanings. Which eight provinces the rays stand for differs between sources (Wikipedia: seven provinces plus Morong; others include Manila or Bataan). Flag text is 441 characters.

flag.text: Toh Chin Chye's committee designed the flag, adopted on 3 December 1959 with self-government, and kept at independence in 1965. Officially, red stands for universal fellowship and equality, white for purity and virtue, the crescent for a young nation on the rise, and the five stars for democracy, peace, progress, justice and equality. Lee Kuan Yew wrote that the Chinese wanted stars and the Malays a crescent, so both were used.

reasons.why: Adopted 3 December 1959 when Singapore gained self-government, designed in about two months by a committee led by deputy prime minister Toh Chin Chye; retained unchanged at independence on 9 August 1965. Confirmed on the Wikipedia flag article.
Official meaning (Wikipedia attributes it to the National Symbols Act; the National Heritage Board's older wording is 'universal brotherhood and equality of man'): universal fellowship and equality.
Official meaning: pervading and everlasting purity and virtue.

reasons.feature: White crescent moon in the upper left

reasons.why: Official meaning: the nation's ideals of democracy, peace, progress, justice and equality.

reasons.feature: Why a crescent and stars together
reasons.why: Lee Kuan Yew's memoir The Singapore Story: the Chinese majority wanted stars (as on China's flag) and the Malay minority wanted a crescent, so both were combined; the design went from three stars to five with a crescent to avoid association with the Malayan Communist Party's three-star symbol and to reassure the Malay community.

flag.text: The flag grew out of the banner of Fretilin, the movement that declared independence from Portugal on 28 November 1975. It was raised again on 20 May 2002, when independence was restored, and the constitution fixes its meaning: yellow for the traces of colonialism, black for the ignorance that must be overcome, red for the struggle for national liberation, and the white star for the light that guides, with white meaning peace.

reasons.why: Derived from the Fretilin party flag; used from the unilateral declaration of independence on 28 November 1975 and formally adopted on 20 May 2002 when independence was restored. Resistance fighter Natalino Leitão is credited (per a widely repeated account) with drawing the national version from the Fretilin flag the night before the 1975 proclamation.
Constitution Section 15(2): red means the struggle for national liberation.
Constitution Section 15(2): yellow means the traces of colonialism in the country's history.
Constitution Section 15(2): black means the obscurantism that needs to be overcome (rendered as 'ignorance' for young readers).

flag.text: King Amanullah chose black, red and green in 1928; the 2004 constitution kept the bands with the white emblem. No law fixes a meaning; black is often read as the past, red as blood shed for freedom, green as hope or Islam. The emblem shows a mosque, two flags, wheat, a rising sun with the Islamic creed and the year 1298, or 1919, when Afghanistan won independence. Since 2021 Kabul's authorities have flown a white flag with the Shahada.

reasons.feature: Three upright bands of black, red and green
reasons.why: The black-red-green combination was introduced by King Amanullah in 1928 (Wikipedia reports an early horizontal arrangement and suggests German inspiration; that detail was not re-verified on review); Article 19 of the 2004 constitution fixes the three equal vertical bands in this order with the emblem in the center.

reasons.feature: Meaning of black, red and green
reasons.why: The constitution gives the colors no meaning. Common readings cited by Wikipedia: black for the troubled 19th-century past under British protection, red for the blood of those who fought for independence (1919), green for hope and prosperity or for Islam.

reasons.feature: White emblem: mosque with prayer niche and pulpit, two small flags, wheat sheaves, rising sun, Shahada and Takbir, word Afghanistan
reasons.why: Article 19 of the 2004 constitution lists every element: a mihrab and pulpit in white, two flags at the corners, the holy phrase (declaration of faith and 'God is great') over the rays of a rising sun, the word Afghanistan and the year, encircled by sheaves of wheat. All of these are visible in the flag image at /tmp/flagwork/out/af.png.
1298 in the Solar Hijri calendar is 1919, the year of the Anglo-Afghan Treaty that ended British control of Afghanistan's foreign affairs, i.e. independence; the constitution names the year.

reasons.why: Since August 2021 the Taliban authorities in Kabul fly a white flag bearing the Shahada, white being said to mean purity of faith; the tricolour remains in use at the UN, by many embassies and at the Olympics. Included as one neutral clause per the owner rule.

flag.text: Adopted on 17 January 1972 after independence from Pakistan, it comes from a flag students made in 1970 and first raised at Dhaka University in March 1971; that flag also carried a yellow map of the country, dropped in 1972. The red circle is often said to stand for the sun rising over Bengal and the blood of those killed in the 1971 war, the green for the lush land. The circle sits a little toward the flagpole so it looks centered when flying.

reasons.feature: Green flag with a red disc, adopted 17 January 1972
reasons.why: Officially adopted on 17 January 1972, weeks after independence (confirmed on review from the Wikipedia flag article); the People's Republic of Bangladesh Flag Rules, 1972 set the proportions, colors and placement.

The first version was designed and made by student leaders of the Swadhin Bangla Nucleus on 6 June 1970 at Iqbal Hall, Dhaka University, and first hoisted there on 2 March 1971 by student leader A. S. M. Abdur Rab, before the war began on 26 March. It carried a yellow map of the country inside the red disc, painted by Shib Narayan Das. On 13 January 1972 the map was removed and the disc moved toward the pole; artist Quamrul Hassan is credited with the 1972 design in the draft, a credit the reviewer's fetch did not surface, so his name was taken out of the flag text.

Wikipedia, citing the CIA World Factbook, says the red circle, reminiscent of the rising sun, represents the sacrifice (blood) of the people during the 1971 Liberation War. No Bangladesh government page stating this was opened, so it is hedged as 'often said'.
Said to symbolize the lush landscape of Bangladesh (Wikipedia, citing the CIA World Factbook); 'youth and progress' is an alternative reading.

reasons.feature: Disc placed slightly toward the flagpole side
reasons.why: The flag rules place the disc off-center toward the pole; Wikipedia states this was done so that it appears centred when the flag is flying. Visible in the image at /tmp/flagwork/out/bd.png.

flag.text: A dragon has stood for Bhutan's name, Druk Yul, land of the thunder dragon, on its flag since 1949; today's design dates from 1969. By the constitution, the upper yellow stands for the king and civil tradition, the lower orange for Buddhist spiritual tradition, and the white dragon for the people's pure thoughts and unity. The jewels in its claws mean wealth and safety, and its snarling mouth the gods said to protect Bhutan.

reasons.why: The 2008 constitution's First Schedule (restating National Assembly Resolution 28 of 1972) says the dragon alludes to the country's Dzongkha name Druk Yul, the Thunder Dragon Kingdom, and to the Drukpa lineage of Buddhism; its placement over the dividing line signifies the equal importance of civic and monastic traditions. Historically the design is credited to Mayum Choying Wangmo Dorji (1947) and was introduced in 1949 with a green dragon on yellow and red; the dragon became white in 1956, red was changed to orange in 1968-69 and the present 2:3 shape was adopted in 1969 (confirmed on review from the Wikipedia flag article).

Per the 1972 resolution and the constitution's First Schedule, yellow signifies civil tradition and temporal authority as embodied in the Druk Gyalpo (Dragon King), whose royal dress traditionally includes a yellow scarf.
Per the same sources, orange signifies the Buddhist spiritual tradition, particularly the Drukpa Kagyu and Nyingma schools. Orange replaced the original red in 1968-69.

Per the 1972 resolution as restated in the constitution's First Schedule, the dragon's white color signifies the purity of inner thoughts and deeds that unite all the ethnically and linguistically diverse peoples of Bhutan (confirmed on review; the text was changed from 'loyalty' to 'unity' to match).

reasons.feature: Jewels (norbu) held in the dragon's claws
reasons.why: Per the 1972 National Assembly Resolution 28 as summarized by Wikipedia, the jewels represent Bhutan's wealth and the security and protection of its people. Visible in all four claws in the image at /tmp/flagwork/out/bt.png.

Per the same 1972 resolution, the snarling mouth symbolizes the Bhutanese deities' commitment to the defence of Bhutan; worded in the text as 'the gods said to protect Bhutan' to report the belief without endorsing it.

entries.remainingDoubts: The jewel and snarling-mouth meanings rest on Wikipedia's summary of the 1972 National Assembly resolution; the constitution text itself was not re-opened on review. flag.text: Green, white and red have been Iran's colors since the early 1900s. Green is often said to mean Islam, white peace and red courage. After the 1979 revolution a red emblem by Hamid Nadimi replaced the old lion and sun in 1980: four crescents and a sword that spell the word Allah. Along the green and red bands the words Allahu Akbar appear 22 times, recalling 22 Bahman, the Iranian calendar date when the revolution won.

reasons.feature: Three horizontal bands of green, white and red
reasons.why: The green-white-red arrangement appeared during the Constitutional Revolution (1905-07) and was formally described in the Supplementary Fundamental Laws of 7 October 1907; Article 18 of the 1979 constitution keeps the same three colors. Wikipedia calls them pan-Iranian colors historically tied to national identity.

Commonly explained as the color of Islam (also growth); the constitution names the color but assigns no meaning, and the Wikipedia flag article gives no per-color meaning, so this is a popular reading.
Commonly explained as peace; not defined in law.
Commonly explained as courage or valor (sometimes martyrdom); not defined in law.

Designed by Hamid Nadimi and required by Article 18 of the constitution as the special emblem of the Islamic Republic; it is made of four crescents and a sword topped by a shadda mark, together forming the Arabic word Allah. It replaced the lion and sun of the monarchy after the 1979 revolution; the flag with it was adopted in July 1980 (confirmed on the Wikipedia flag article).

reasons.feature: White Kufic writing along the inner edges of the green and red bands
reasons.why: The phrase Allahu Akbar (God is greatest), the motto named in Article 18, written 11 times on each band, 22 in all, to recall 22 Bahman (11 February 1979), the day the revolution succeeded. Count and reason confirmed on the Wikipedia flag article.

entries.remainingDoubts: Population comes from Worldometers' copy of WPP 2024 rather than the UN portal itself (API returned 401) and was not re-fetched in this pass. The emblem is also often described as resembling a tulip (a martyrdom symbol); not included because no cited source confirmed it. flag.text: Maldivian ships long flew a plain red flag, and red is now said to recall those who died for the country. Between 1926 and 1932 a white crescent on a green panel was added; green is said to mean peace and prosperity, and the crescent is said to stand for Islam, the state religion. A black and white striped strip ran along the pole side until 1965, when the Maldives became independent from Britain and adopted today's flag.

reasons.why: The earliest Maldivian flag was a plain red one, like many flags around the Indian Ocean and Arabia; the red border keeps that tradition. Wikipedia says it represents the blood of the nation's heroes and their willingness to sacrifice, but no flag law stating this was found, so it is given as a popular reading.

A distinct state flag with the crescent on a green panel appeared in the same period as the crescent (1926-1932); green is commonly said to mean peace and prosperity (Britannica also links it, with the crescent, to progress). No law giving the meaning was found.

reasons.feature: White crescent, opening toward the free end of the flag

reasons.feature: Overall design without the old black-and-white pole-side stripe

flag.text: Nepal's flag is the only national flag that is not a rectangle: two stacked pennants once flown separately by branches of the ruling family. Crimson, the color of the rhododendron, Nepal's national flower, is often said to mean bravery; the blue border is said to mean peace. The moon and sun had human faces until 1962, when the constitution fixed today's design; they are often read as a wish that Nepal will last as long as they do.

reasons.why: The design combines two single pennants historically used by rival branches of the ruling dynasty; tradition credits King Prithvi Narayan Shah with joining them after unifying Nepal in the 18th century. Wikipedia and Britannica state it is the only non-rectangular national flag and the only one taller than it is wide. Popular accounts tie the two points to the Himalayas or to Hinduism and Buddhism, but these are readings rather than documented origins.

Crimson is the color of the rhododendron, the national flower, and is commonly said to mean the bravery of the Nepali people; Britannica notes crimson and blue are simply popular colors in Nepalese art. The constitution specifies the color but gives no meaning (Wikipedia calls the meanings modern interpretations).
Commonly said to represent peace and harmony; no official meaning is given.

reasons.feature: White moon with rays in the upper pennant
reasons.why: Historically the Rana rulers used the moon and sun for the lunar and solar dynasties (moon for the royal house); modern readings link the moon to peace and the cool Himalayas, and with the sun to the hope that Nepal will endure as long as the sun and moon.

reasons.feature: White twelve-pointed sun in the lower pennant
reasons.why: Traditionally linked to the Rana prime-ministerial family (solar dynasty) and to the heat and hard work of the southern lowlands, and with the moon to the wish for permanence.

reasons.feature: Sun and moon without faces; exact proportions
reasons.why: Earlier versions showed human faces on both; the present faceless design was adopted on 16 December 1962 under that year's constitution (confirmed on the Wikipedia flag article), and the Constitution of Nepal 2015 (Article 8 and Schedule 1) prescribes the flag with step-by-step drawing instructions.

reasons.feature: Gold border around the whole flag and between the two panels

flag.text: Armenia's First Republic adopted the red, blue and orange bands on 1 August 1918, as proposed by scholar Stepan Malkhasyants; they returned on 24 August 1990 as Soviet rule ended. Officially, red stands for the Armenian Highland, the people's struggle to survive, their Christian faith and freedom; blue for the wish to live under peaceful skies; and orange for creative talent and hard work. In 1918 they were read as blood, sky and talent.

reasons.feature: Three equal horizontal bands of red, blue and orange
reasons.why: Adopted on 1 August 1918 by the First Republic of Armenia on a proposal by Stepan Malkhasyants (per Simon Vratsian's account), dropped under Soviet rule, and readopted on 24 August 1990 by the Armenian Supreme Soviet; the 2006 Law on the National Flag (HO-149) describes the three equal stripes.

The 2006 Law on the National Flag, as quoted on Wikipedia and on the president's website, states red emblematizes the Armenian Highland, the Armenian people's continued struggle for survival, maintenance of the Christian faith, and Armenia's independence and freedom.
The 2006 Law on the National Flag, as quoted on Wikipedia and on the president's website, states blue emblematizes the will of the people of Armenia to live beneath peaceful skies.

The 2006 Law on the National Flag, as quoted on Wikipedia and on the president's website, states orange emblematizes the creative talent and hard-working nature of the people of Armenia. Historically, some 1918 parliament members wanted green instead because orange cloth was hard to find, but Prime Minister Hovhannes Kajaznuni kept orange as more pleasing to the eye.

reasons.feature: 1918 reading of the colors as blood, sky and talent

flag.text: Bahrain long flew a plain red flag, a traditional color of Gulf Arab states. After an 1820 peace treaty with Britain, a white band was added at the left edge to set it apart from pirate flags. The zigzag edge came in the 1930s to tell it from neighbors' flags. A royal decree of 14 February 2002 fixed the white points at five, which the government links to the Five Pillars of Islam. Red is often said to recall past battles, white peace.

reasons.feature: Red area filling most of the flag
reasons.why: Before 1820 Bahrain's flag was plain red, the color traditionally used by Arab rulers of the Gulf; Britannica links it to the Kharijite branch of Islam that once controlled the area.

reasons.feature: White band along the left edge
reasons.why: Added after Bahrain signed the 1820 General Maritime Treaty with the British Empire, to signify the treaty and distinguish the flag from those commonly used by pirates; Bahrain chose a narrow strip at the pole side rather than a full white border.

reasons.feature: Zigzag (serrated) line between white and red
reasons.why: Introduced in the 1930s (Wikipedia says 1932; Britannica dates formal recognition to 1933) to differentiate Bahrain's flag from neighbors' similar red-and-white flags. The points were cut from 28 to 8 in 1972.
On 14 February 2002 Decree-Law No. 4 of 2002, issued by King Hamad, reduced the serration from eight to five triangles so that each point could stand for one of the Five Pillars of Islam.
Wikipedia states red represents the blood of the martyrs and the battles of Bahrain, and white is popularly read as peace; these are customary readings rather than a legal definition.

flag.text: Cyprus adopted this flag at independence in 1960. Its constitution required a neutral design, so it avoids the blue of Greece and the red of Turkey and has no cross or crescent. The cross of St. George, patron saint of Georgia; the Pizzigano map of 1367 shows a red-on-white Jerusalem-type cross as the flag of the Kingdom of Georgia (Wikipedia, confirmed this session), and a coin of King David IV carries a five-cross composition per the State Council of Heraldry (FOTW).

flag.text: Adopted in 1928, Jordan's flag comes from the flag of the 1916 Arab Revolt against Ottoman rule, the source of the Pan-Arab colors. The white seven-pointed star stands for Arab unity, its points linked to the seven verses of the Quran's opening chapter.

Government explanation (and Wikipedia): the red triangle joining the bands represents the Hashemite dynasty, which led the Arab Revolt and rules Jordan.

flag.text: Lebanon's flag entered the constitution on 7 December 1943. Members of parliament sketched it during protests against French rule, replacing a French-style blue, white and red flag; Henri Pharaon said Austria's red and white inspired the bands. The cedar, Lebanon's age-old symbol, stayed and must be all green. No law gives meanings, but red is often said to recall blood shed for freedom, white peace and mountain snow, and the cedar long life.

reasons.feature: Designed during the independence crisis of November 1943

The text therefore attributes the Austrian link to Pharaon's own account rather than stating it as fact.

reasons.feature: Replacement of the earlier French-style flag

flag.text: Syria's flag is the independence flag, first flown in the early 1930s under French rule and kept after independence in 1946. Britannica: the crescent (and star) was taken over by Muslim Turkic peoples from Constantinople, where it predated Islam; this is an origin story rather than a documented act, so the text says 'often traced to'.

Turkish Flag Law No. 2994 of 29 May 1936 set measures, proportions and the exact tone of red; Law No. 2893 of 22 September 1983 replaced it and governs the flag (Britannica dates the 1936 reconfirmation to 5 June 1936).

Neither the flag law nor Britannica gives an official meaning; the association with the blood of martyrs is described as traditional folklore, and Britannica says the various myths do not explain the origins.

flag.text: The flag was first raised on 2 December 1971, the day the United Arab Emirates was formed. The designer said black stands for oil and green for fertile gardens, while the red upright band and the white come from the emirates' own flags.

flag.text: Adopted on 22 May 1990, when North and South Yemen united, the flag uses the red, white and black bands of the Arab Liberation flag, begun in Egypt in 1952 and shared with Syria and Iraq. North Yemen's flag had a green star and South Yemen's a blue triangle with a red star; the joint flag dropped both. Red is often said to stand for the blood shed for independence and unity, white for a bright future and black for the dark past.

reasons.feature: Three horizontal bands of red, white and black
reasons.why: The design is the Arab Liberation Flag that arose from Egypt's 1952 revolution and spread to other Arab republics (Egypt, Syria, Iraq, Sudan); Wikipedia states it served as the derivation for the flags of both North and South Yemen before unification.

reasons.why: North Yemen's flag (adopted 1 November 1962) had a green five-pointed star in the center, and South Yemen's flag (adopted 30 November 1967) had a light blue triangle at the pole side with a red star for the National Liberation Front; these distinguishing elements were removed when the two states united and adopted the common plain three-band flag on 22 May 1990.

The flag was adopted on the day the Yemen Arab Republic (north) and the People's Democratic Republic of Yemen (south) merged into the Republic of Yemen; Wikipedia cites Presidency Council Resolution No. (1) of 1990 Regarding the National Flag as the legal instrument defining it, and Britannica confirms the simple three-band flag has been used since May 22, 1990.
